\chapter{Dancing, and the Article You Drop}
\label{ch:bailar}
\hlchaptermodality{419}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say that I like dancing, dropping the article before the infinitive that I keep before the noun.}

Say both halves in one breath: me gusta la musica y me gusta bailar, and notice that la was said once and not twice.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[bailar]{bailar — and the verb that needs no article}

\label{lesson:ES-C419-bailar}



\begin{quote}
You have met \emph{me gusta \textbf{la} música}, which keeps an article English throws away. Hold that thought — this lesson is the case where the rule switches off.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{What to know first}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item música — the noun this verb belongs with, and the article rule this lesson contrasts against.
\end{itemize}

\begin{sounds}
\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \texttt{diphthong-ai} — \textbf{ai} is one syllable, \emph{bai-}, close to English \emph{bye}. $\to$ reference
  \item \texttt{b-soft} — the \textbf{b} is softer than an English \emph{b}; the lips barely close.
  \item \texttt{r-tap} — the final \textbf{r} is a single flick of the tongue, not a growl.
\end{itemize}
\end{sounds}

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{bailar} — \textquotedblleft{}to dance.\textquotedblright{} An \emph{-ar} infinitive, the most ordinary shape a Spanish verb can have.

Root: Late Latin \textbf{ballare}, \textquotedblleft{}to dance,\textquotedblright{} from Greek \emph{ballízein}. This root travelled further into English than almost any other on this page:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item a \textbf{ball} — the \emph{dancing} kind. A ballroom is a room for \emph{ballare}.
  \item \textbf{ball}et — through Italian \emph{balletto}, \textquotedblleft{}a little dance.\textquotedblright{}
  \item \textbf{ball}ad — Provençal \emph{balada}, originally a \textbf{song you danced to}. That is why a ballad tells a story in verses: the verses were danced.
\end{itemize}

And now the trap worth knowing, because it looks like the strongest member of the family and is not:

\begin{quote}
A \textbf{ball} you \emph{throw} is not related. That one is Germanic, a cousin of \emph{balloon} and \emph{bowl}. English has two unrelated words spelled \emph{ball}, and only the one you dance at comes from \emph{ballare}.
\end{quote}
\end{cousinweb}

\begin{grammarlens}[title={Grammar Lens: where the article rule switches off}]
Put the two halves of this chapter side by side:

\begin{quote}
\emph{Me gusta \textbf{la} música.} — I like music. \textbf{Article.} \emph{Me gusta bailar.} — I like dancing. \textbf{No article.}
\end{quote}

This is not an exception to memorise; it follows from what \emph{gustar} does. It needs a subject, and an infinitive is already one — \emph{bailar} means \textquotedblleft{}to dance,\textquotedblright{} a whole action named. A \textbf{noun} needs its article to be spoken of in general; a \textbf{verb} does not, because naming it is what the infinitive is for.

So: if what pleases you is a thing, it takes \emph{el} or \emph{la}. If what pleases you is an action, the bare infinitive is the whole answer.
\end{grammarlens}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}bailar\textquotedblright{} — one flick of the tongue on the final \emph{r}
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me gusta bailar\textquotedblright{} — I like dancing, with no article
  \item \textquotedblleft{}me gusta la música y me gusta bailar\textquotedblright{} — both halves, and notice you said \emph{la} once and not twice
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Why does \emph{me gusta la música} take \emph{la} while \emph{me gusta bailar} takes nothing? (A noun needs its article to mean the thing in general; an infinitive already names the action.) Which English \emph{ball} comes from this root — the dance or the thing you throw? (The dance.)
\end{tcolorbox}
